baseline: Host Linux 6.8.0-124 with the pinned LTP 20260529 binary: 44 passed, 0 failed, 0 broken, 0 skipped. The test runs 11 cases across 4 variants (the 2 time64 variants are compiled out on x86_64 because __NR_clock_getres_time64 is not defined there). Per assertion, measured directly with raw syscall(SYS_clock_getres, ...) on the host: clock ids 0 REALTIME, 1 MONOTONIC, 2 PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID, 3 THREAD_CPUTIME_ID, 4 MONOTONIC_RAW, 7 BOOTTIME, 8 REALTIME_ALARM and 9 BOOTTIME_ALARM all return 0 with res = {0 sec, 1 nsec}; ids 5 REALTIME_COARSE and 6 MONOTONIC_COARSE return 0 with res = {0 sec, 1000000 nsec}; clockid -1 returns -1/EINVAL. A NULL res pointer succeeds (returns 0, writes nothing) for a valid clock, and still returns EINVAL for clockid -1 -- validation precedes the copy-out. Confirmed under strace that glibc serves ids 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7 from the vDSO without entering the kernel, and issues the real syscall only for 2, 3, 8, 9 and -1. That split is what makes the Asterinas result partial rather than total.
failing_assertion: In Asterinas at base e8f2b9ca6 the run reports 12 passed / 10 failed / 2 skipped (24 results, not 44), and make run_kernel exits 1 with 'clock_getres01: fail'. The 10 failures are, in each of the 2 libc variants, the 5 cases that reach a real syscall: clock_getres(PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID), (THREAD_CPUTIME_ID), (CLOCK_REALTIME_ALARM), (CLOCK_BOOTTIME_ALARM) and (-1). All 5 return -1 with errno = ENOSYS. For the first four the correct value is 0 with res = {0,1}; for -1 the correct errno is EINVAL, and Asterinas's ENOSYS is the wrong value in the very case the test checks an error for -- the test downgrades an EINVAL mismatch to TCONF (clock_getres01.c:72-75) but ENOSYS is not EINVAL, so it becomes TFAIL at clock_getres01.c:77. The 2 skips are the two raw-syscall variants ('syscall with old kernel spec', with and without NULL res): LTP's tst_syscall wrapper turns any ENOSYS into tst_brk(TCONF, 'syscall(229) __NR_clock_getres not supported on your arch'), which aborts the whole variant, which is why 20 of the host's 44 results never run at all. The 12 that do pass never enter the kernel -- they are served by the prebuilt Linux vDSO -- and they pass only because the test checks the return value and errno and never inspects the resolution it was handed.

also: kernel/src/syscall/arch/generic.rs:303-304 -- SYS_CLOCK_GETTIME = 113 is followed directly by SYS_CLOCK_NANOSLEEP = 115; 114 (clock_getres) is absent, so riscv64 has the identical hole
kernel/src/syscall/mod.rs:337-343 -- the syscall_dispatch catch-all arm that turns the absent number into ENOSYS
kernel/src/vdso.rs:101 and 131 -- VdsoData.hrtimer_res is declared and initialised to 0 and never written again; grep over the whole tree finds exactly those two references
kernel/src/time/core/mod.rs:9-12 -- the Clock trait, whose doc comment says a clock 'has a fixed resolution' but which exposes only read_time() and no way to ask for that resolution
kernel/src/syscall/clock_gettime.rs:41-50 and 112-155 -- the ClockId enum and read_clock(), the existing single point where a clockid_t is validated and mapped to a clock

root_cause:
Two distinct defects on the same path, both in code that exists.

(1) The syscall is absent from both dispatch tables. kernel/src/syscall/arch/x86.rs jumps from SYS_CLOCK_GETTIME = 228 (line 360) straight to SYS_CLOCK_NANOSLEEP = 230 (line 361), skipping 229; kernel/src/syscall/arch/generic.rs jumps from 113 (line 303) to 115 (line 304), skipping 114. Because there is no arm for the number, the macro-generated match in kernel/src/syscall/mod.rs falls to its catch-all at lines 337-343, which logs 'Unimplemented syscall number' and returns ENOSYS. That is the mechanism producing errno 9 where the test expects either 0 or EINVAL. Nothing else is wrong with the clocks underneath: sys_clock_gettime passes in the same boot, and read_clock() in kernel/src/syscall/clock_gettime.rs already resolves all 8 positive ClockId variants and already returns EINVAL for an out-of-range positive id (via From<int_to_c_enum::TryFromIntError> at kernel/src/error.rs:348-352) and for the invalid dynamic-clock encoding (kernel/src/syscall/clock_gettime.rs:81-83). The validation the -1 case needs is therefore already written and merely unreachable.

(2) Independently, VdsoData.hrtimer_res (kernel/src/vdso.rs:101) is set to 0 in VdsoData::empty() at line 131 and is never assigned anywhere else -- VdsoData::init() at lines 137-147 sets clock_mode and the coefficients and the basetimes but not hrtimer_res. Asterinas maps a prebuilt Linux vDSO (kernel/src/vdso.rs:224-228) whose __vdso_clock_getres reads exactly that field for the VDSO_HRES and VDSO_RAW clocks. So the 12 cases that currently 'pass' are being told the resolution of CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and CLOCK_BOOTTIME is 0 nanoseconds, where Linux reports 1. clock_getres01 does not read the value so it cannot see this, but it is a live wrong answer to userspace today and it sits on the same path the fix touches. Fixing (1) alone would leave Asterinas returning 1ns via the syscall and 0ns via the vDSO for the same clock -- a self-inconsistency introduced by the fix rather than by the bug.

Why 'bug' and not 'missing-feature': the POSIX clock subsystem this call reports on is fully implemented -- eight clock instances, their validation, and their dispatch all exist and work. What is missing is two table rows and one never-written field, and defect (2) is unambiguously a defect in code that already runs. No new subsystem is required.
invariant: Every clock identifier the kernel accepts for reading a time must also report a resolution, every identifier it rejects must be rejected with the same errno by both operations, and the resolution reported for a given clock must be the same value no matter which path served the request -- syscall or vDSO. A clock's resolution is a property of the clock, not of the call used to ask for it.
owning_layer: The POSIX clock abstraction in kernel/src/time -- the Clock trait in kernel/src/time/core/mod.rs, together with the single clockid_t-to-clock resolution point that read_clock() in kernel/src/syscall/clock_gettime.rs currently owns. Resolution belongs beside read_time() on the clock itself, above the syscall handlers, because three separate consumers need the same number: the new sys_clock_getres, the vDSO hrtimer_res field in kernel/src/vdso.rs, and any future timer-granularity rounding. Asterinas's abstractions do not line up with Linux's here: Linux has a k_clock vtable per clock carrying both .clock_get_timespec and .clock_getres, whereas Asterinas's Clock trait carries only read_time() -- its doc comment already asserts a clock 'has a fixed resolution' but the trait gives no way to obtain it, which is precisely the gap. The narrowest edit that turns this test green is a self-contained sys_clock_getres with a hardcoded match on ClockId, and that is the wrong layer: it duplicates the ClockId dispatch read_clock already performs and leaves the vDSO reporting a different resolution for the same clock.
linux_reference: kernel/time/posix-timers.c, SYSCALL_DEFINE2(clock_getres, ...). Linux enforces the rule in the POSIX clock layer, above the individual clocks and above the syscall entry: clockid_to_kclock(which_clock) is the shared validation point and returning NULL from it is the single source of EINVAL, so clock_gettime and clock_getres cannot disagree about which ids are valid. The resolution itself comes from the per-clock vtable hook kc->clock_getres -- posix_get_hrtimer_res() for the high-resolution clocks, which sets tv_sec = 0, tv_nsec = hrtimer_resolution, and posix_get_coarse_res() for the coarse ones. NULL is legal by construction: the copy-out is guarded by 'if (!error && tp && put_timespec64(...))', so validation strictly precedes and is independent of writing user memory. The vDSO half is __cvdso_clock_getres_common() in lib/vdso/gettimeofday.c, which deliberately mirrors the syscall rather than inventing its own answer -- the comments say so ('Preserves the behaviour of posix_get_hrtimer_res()' / 'posix_get_coarse_res()'): for 1U << clock in VDSO_HRES | VDSO_RAW it reads vd->hrtimer_res, for VDSO_COARSE it uses the LOW_RES_NSEC constant, and anything else returns false and falls back to the syscall. It carries the same 'if (likely(res))' NULL guard. The masks are in include/vdso/datapage.h: VDSO_HRES covers REALTIME, MONOTONIC, BOOTTIME and TAI, VDSO_COARSE covers REALTIME_COARSE and MONOTONIC_COARSE, VDSO_RAW covers MONOTONIC_RAW -- which is exactly the set that bypasses the kernel in the strace above, and exactly the set Asterinas is currently answering with 0. The reference answer is therefore that one authoritative resolution per clock lives in the clock layer and both the syscall and the vDSO data page are populated from it.
other_callers: kernel/src/vdso.rs is already affected and already returning a wrong answer today: hrtimer_res = 0 makes __vdso_clock_getres report 0ns for CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW and CLOCK_BOOTTIME for every process on the system, independently of this test. That is the concrete reason the layer choice matters rather than a hypothetical one. Two further callers resolve a clockid_t through the same ClockId enum and would inherit any change to how that dispatch is factored, though neither needs a resolution value itself: create_timer() in kernel/src/syscall/timer_create.rs:137-143 and sys_timerfd_create in kernel/src/syscall/timerfd_create.rs:13. kernel/src/device/evdev/file.rs:432 also does ClockId::try_from for its timestamp clock. Adjacent but out of scope: clock_settime is missing from both tables too (227 on x86, 112 on generic -- the same kind of hole, verified by the same greps), and Linux's clock_nanosleep rounds to timer granularity using the same resolution constant, which Asterinas has nowhere to read from. On the ALARM clocks the honest answer is that nobody else is affected: CLOCK_REALTIME_ALARM (8) and CLOCK_BOOTTIME_ALARM (9) are not in the ClockId enum at all, and grep finds no ALARM clock support in the kernel, so they will return EINVAL -- which this test explicitly downgrades to TCONF rather than TFAIL, so they need no work.
suggested_direction:
Give the clock layer a resolution, then have all three consumers read it from there.

1. Add a resolution accessor to the Clock trait in kernel/src/time/core/mod.rs -- e.g. fn resolution(&self) -> Duration -- with a 1ns default, overridden to return the coarse tick period on RealTimeCoarseClock and MonotonicCoarseClock in kernel/src/time/clocks/system_wide.rs. Note that Asterinas's coarse clocks are refreshed from the softirq timer, so the honest value is that update period, not a copy of Linux's 1ms; state whichever value is chosen and where it comes from rather than hardcoding 1_000_000.
2. Add kernel/src/syscall/clock_getres.rs with sys_clock_getres(clockid, res_addr, ctx). Resolve the clockid through the same path read_clock() uses so the two calls cannot disagree about validity -- the cleanest shape is to factor the clockid-to-clock lookup out of read_clock() into a shared helper that both call, so the EINVAL behaviour for an out-of-range id and for the invalid dynamic-clock encoding is inherited rather than reimplemented. Validate first, and only then, if res_addr is non-zero, write timespec_t::from(resolution); a null res_addr must return 0 without touching user memory, and an invalid clockid must return EINVAL whether or not res_addr is null. Two of the four live variants pass NULL, so this is load-bearing, not defensive.
3. Register it in both tables: SYS_CLOCK_GETRES = 229 between lines 360 and 361 of kernel/src/syscall/arch/x86.rs, and SYS_CLOCK_GETRES = 114 between lines 303 and 304 of kernel/src/syscall/arch/generic.rs. Add the mod declaration in kernel/src/syscall/mod.rs and the use in both arch files, matching how clock_gettime is wired.
4. Populate VdsoData.hrtimer_res in VdsoData::init() (kernel/src/vdso.rs:137-147) from the same clock-layer value, so the vDSO and the syscall agree. Without this step the fix makes Asterinas self-inconsistent: 1ns from the syscall, 0ns from the vDSO, for the same clock.

Expected result: the two raw-syscall variants stop aborting with TCONF and run their 11 cases each, the four syscall-served ids return 0, clockid -1 returns EINVAL, and ids 8 and 9 return EINVAL which the test records as TCONF. Do not expect 44/44 -- the ALARM clocks are unimplemented, so the realistic green result is 42 passed / 0 failed / 2 conf. What matters for the suite is failed = 0 and broken = 0, which is what run_ltp_test.sh checks. Worth verifying after the fix that the resolution actually handed back is 1ns and not 0 on both paths, since this test would not catch a 0.
